claim: A small subset of interneurons that are generated earliest as pioneer neurons are the first cohort of neurons that enter the neocortex.
source: A small subset of interneurons that are generated earliest as pioneer neurons are the first cohort of neurons that enter the neocortex.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that references established knowledge about pioneer neurons in the neocortex.

claim: EGIns exhibited more mature electrophysiological and morphological properties than pRIns in the somatosensory cortex at early postnatal stages.
source: Using inducible genetic fate mapping to selectively label EGIns and pseudo-random interneurons (pRIns), we found that EGIns exhibited more mature electrophysiological and morphological properties and higher synaptic connectivity than pRIns in the somatosensory cortex at early postnatal stages.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from electrophysiological recordings and morphological analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: EGIns exhibited higher synaptic connectivity than pRIns in the somatosensory cortex at early postnatal stages.
source: Using inducible genetic fate mapping to selectively label EGIns and pseudo-random interneurons (pRIns), we found that EGIns exhibited more mature electrophysiological and morphological properties and higher synaptic connectivity than pRIns in the somatosensory cortex at early postnatal stages.
evidence: This claim is supported by dual whole-cell patch-clamp recording data showing connection probabilities.

claim: The proportion of EGIns that influence spontaneous network synchronization is significantly higher than that of pRIns when stimulating one cell.
source: In addition, when stimulating one cell, the proportion of EGIns that influence spontaneous network synchronization is significantly higher than that of pRIns.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from dual patch-clamp recordings measuring GDP frequency changes.

claim: Toxin-mediated ablation of EGIns after birth significantly reduces spontaneous network synchronization during the first postnatal week.
source: Importantly, toxin-mediated ablation of EGIns after birth significantly reduce spontaneous network synchronization and decrease inhibitory synaptic formation during the first postnatal week.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from DT-mediated ablation experiments measuring GDP frequency.

claim: Toxin-mediated ablation of EGIns after birth decreases inhibitory synaptic formation during the first postnatal week.
source: Importantly, toxin-mediated ablation of EGIns after birth significantly reduce spontaneous network synchronization and decrease inhibitory synaptic formation during the first postnatal week.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mIPSC recordings in pyramidal neurons after EGIn ablation.

claim: EGIns can shape developing networks and may contribute to the refinement of neuronal connectivity before the establishment of the adult neuronal circuit.
source: These results suggest that EGIns can shape developing networks and may contribute to the reﬁnement of neuronal connectivity before the establishment of the adult neuronal circuit.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results presented in the study.

claim: GABAergic inhibitory interneurons comprise approximately 20% of the neuronal population in the neocortex.
source: γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA)-ergic inhibitory interneurons comprise ~20% of the neuronal population in the neocortex.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the composition of the neocortex.

claim: Interneurons exhibit incredibly rich diversity in their morphology, biochemical marker expression, electrophysiological properties and synaptic connectivity patterns.
source: A key feature of these interneurons is the incredibly rich diversity in their morphology, biochemical marker expression, electrophysiological properties and synaptic connectivity patterns (Ascoli et al., 2008), which allows them to dynamically sculpt neuronal activity and network oscillations both during development and upon maturation (Liguz-Lecznar et al., 2016; Whittington and Traub, 2003), and endow neural circuits with remarkable computational power (Kepecs and Fishell, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Interneurons dynamically sculpt neuronal activity and network oscillations both during development and upon maturation.
source: A key feature of these interneurons is the incredibly rich diversity in their morphology, biochemical marker expression, electrophysiological properties and synaptic connectivity patterns (Ascoli et al., 2008), which allows them to dynamically sculpt neuronal activity and network oscillations both during development and upon maturation (Liguz-Lecznar et al., 2016; Whittington and Traub, 2003), and endow neural circuits with remarkable computational power (Kepecs and Fishell, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Interneurons endow neural circuits with remarkable computational power.
source: A key feature of these interneurons is the incredibly rich diversity in their morphology, biochemical marker expression, electrophysiological properties and synaptic connectivity patterns (Ascoli et al., 2008), which allows them to dynamically sculpt neuronal activity and network oscillations both during development and upon maturation (Liguz-Lecznar et al., 2016; Whittington and Traub, 2003), and endow neural circuits with remarkable computational power (Kepecs and Fishell, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: GABAergic interneurons play crucial roles in several aspects of neural circuit development, including circuit formation and maturation, and synaptic plasticity.
source: Considerable evidence suggests that GABAergic interneurons play crucial roles in several aspects of neural circuit development, including circuit formation and maturation, and synaptic plasticity (Anastasiades et al., 2016; Dehorter et al., 2017; Le Magueresse and Monyer, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Disruption of the early-born SST interneurons located in cortical layer 5/6 during the first postnatal week impedes the synaptic maturation of thalamocortical inputs onto infragranular PV interneurons.
source: For example, disruption of the early-born SST interneurons located in cortical layer 5/6 during the first postnatal week impedes the synaptic maturation of thalamocortical inputs onto infragranular PV interneurons (Tuncdemir et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Developmental dysfunction of VIP interneurons by deletion of ErbB4 from these cells causes long-term defects in excitatory and inhibitory cortical neurons and impairs sensory processing and perception.
source: A recent study has also shown that developmental dysfunction of VIP interneurons by deletion of ErbB4 from these cells causes long-term defects in excitatory and inhibitory cortical neurons and impairs sensory processing and perception (Batista-Brito et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Disruption of the developing GABAergic neocortical inhibitory network has been implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders, including schizophrenia, epilepsy, and autism.
source: Disruption of the developing GABAergic neocortical inhibitory network has been implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders, including schizophrenia, epilepsy, and autism (Cobos et al., 2005; Lewis et al., 2005; Pizzarelli and Cherubini, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The generation of neocortical interneurons begins at embryonic day (E) 9.5 in mice.
source: The generation of neocortical interneurons begins at embryonic day (E) 9.5, peaks at E12 to E15 and ends at E18.5 in mice (Batista-Brito and Fishell, 2009; Miyoshi et al., 2010; Miyoshi et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The generation of neocortical interneurons peaks at E12 to E15 in mice.
source: The generation of neocortical interneurons begins at embryonic day (E) 9.5, peaks at E12 to E15 and ends at E18.5 in mice (Batista-Brito and Fishell, 2009; Miyoshi et al., 2010; Miyoshi et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The generation of neocortical interneurons ends at E18.5 in mice.
source: The generation of neocortical interneurons begins at embryonic day (E) 9.5, peaks at E12 to E15 and ends at E18.5 in mice (Batista-Brito and Fishell, 2009; Miyoshi et al., 2010; Miyoshi et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Each temporal cohort of interneurons exhibits specific physiological properties based on their birthdate and has distinct functional roles in the neocortex.
source: Each temporal cohort exhibits specific physiological properties based on their birthdate and has distinct functional roles in the neocortex (Butt et al., 2005; Donato et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The earliest generated cohort is a unique subpopulation of interneurons.
source: Among these temporal cohorts, accumulating evidence suggests that the earliest generated cohort is a unique subpopulation of interneurons (Allene et al., 2012; Picardo et al., 2011; Tuncdemir et al., 2016; Villette et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Early emerging individuals in a network have a strong 'first-mover advantage' based on the preferential attachment rule.
source: Based on the preferential attachment rule that early emerging individuals in a network have a strong 'first-mover advantage' (Barabasi and Albert, 1999), it has long been postulated that early-generated interneurons (EGIns) may develop a subpopulation of functional hub neurons and play a key role in regulating neural development, neuronal network dynamics and circuit formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature on network theory.

claim: It has long been postulated that early-generated interneurons may develop a subpopulation of functional hub neurons and play a key role in regulating neural development, neuronal network dynamics and circuit formation.
source: Based on the preferential attachment rule that early emerging individuals in a network have a strong 'first-mover advantage' (Barabasi and Albert, 1999), it has long been postulated that early-generated interneurons (EGIns) may develop a subpopulation of functional hub neurons and play a key role in regulating neural development, neuronal network dynamics and circuit formation.
evidence: This is a statement about a hypothesis in the field, supported by inference from network theory.

claim: A subpopulation of EGIns in the developing hippocampus and entorhinal cortex displays high functional connectivity and serves as functional hub cells by exerting a powerful effect on network synchronization at the end of the first postnatal week.
source: Indeed, genetic fate mapping studies have shown that a subpopulation of EGIns in the developing hippocampus and entorhinal cortex displays high functional connectivity and serves as functional hub cells by exerting a powerful effect on network synchronization at the end of the first postnatal week (Bonifazi et al., 2009; Cossart, 2014; Mòdol et al., 2017; Picardo et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: GABAergic hub neurons are characterized by an exceptionally widespread axonal arborization and preferentially express somatostatin.
source: In addition, GABAergic hub neurons are characterized by an exceptionally widespread axonal arborization and preferentially express somatostatin (Cossart, 2014; Mòdol et al., 2017; Picardo et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Dlx1/2 is a transcription factor that is transiently expressed in almost all forebrain interneurons as they become postmitotic.
source: Dlx1/2 is a transcription factor that is transiently expressed in almost all forebrain interneurons as they become postmitotic (Eisenstat et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The tamoxifen efficacy lasts no longer than two days in the Dlx1/2-CreER fate-mapping approach.
source: To confirm the temporal resolution of our fate-mapping approach, we administered a tamoxifen solution (0.06 mg/g) by oral gavage to pregnant Dlx1/2-CreER+/-; Rosa26-EYFP ± mice at E13.5, followed by a single 5-bromo-2'-deoxyuridine (BrdU) i.p. injection at E15.5, and detected few BrdU+/EYFP+ cells in the somatosensory cortex at P6 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B). This result indicates that the tamoxifen efficacy lasts no longer than two days.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from BrdU labeling experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: 1.6 ± 0.3% of EYFP+ cells were positive for BrdU in the somatosensory cortex of Dlx1/2-CreER+/-; Rosa26-EYFP ± mice at P5 that were gavaged with tamoxifen at E9.5 and injected BrdU at E13.5.
source: Similarly, 1.6 ± 0.3% of EYFP+ cells (n = 20 sections from four mice) were positive for BrdU in the somatosensory cortex of Dlx1/2-CreER+/-; Rosa26-EYFP ± mice at P5 that were gavaged with tamoxifen at E9.5 and injected BrdU at E13.5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D), suggesting that EGIns and pRIns are two temporally separated cohorts.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from BrdU labeling experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: EGIns and pRIns are two temporally separated cohorts.
source: Similarly, 1.6 ± 0.3% of EYFP+ cells (n = 20 sections from four mice) were positive for BrdU in the somatosensory cortex of Dlx1/2-CreER+/-; Rosa26-EYFP ± mice at P5 that were gavaged with tamoxifen at E9.5 and injected BrdU at E13.5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D), suggesting that EGIns and pRIns are two temporally separated cohorts.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the BrdU labeling data showing minimal overlap between the two populations.

claim: The majority of Dlx1/2-EYFP+ cells at E11 were OLIG2-/Ki67- (100%).
source: We found the majority of Dlx1/2-EYFP+ cells at E11 and E15 were OLIG2-/Ki67- (100% at E11, n = 9 sections from three embryos; 99.5 ± 0.5% at E15, n = 12 sections from four embryos) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), indicating that Dlx1/2-CreER line predominantly labels post-mitotic interneurons at the embryonic stage.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: 99.5 ± 0.5% of Dlx1/2-EYFP+ cells at E15 were OLIG2-/Ki67-.

claim: The density of pRIns was approximately 14 times higher than that of EGIns in the neocortex at P30.
source: The density of pRIns was approximately 14 times higher than that of EGIns in the neocortex (pRIns, 41.4 ± 2.0 cells/mm2, n = 25 sections from six mice; EGIns, 3.0 ± 0.2 cells/mm2, n = 28 sections from seven mice; Figure 1—source data 1), indicating that EGIns are a very sparse population of cortical interneurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from cell density measurements.

claim: EGIns are a very sparse population of cortical interneurons.

claim: EGIns included approximately 10% of leaky EYFP+ cells in immunohistochemical cortical sections.
source: Of note, consistent with previous report (Lim et al., 2018; Villette et al., 2016), we found EGIns included approximately 10% of leaky EYFP+ cells in immunohistochemical cortical sections, but none in live cortical slices.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from immunohistochemistry and is consistent with previous reports.

claim: Both EGIns and pRIns exhibited a location bias towards infragranular layers (layer 5–6, L5/6).
source: Both EGIns and pRIns exhibited a location bias towards infragranular layers (layer 5–6, L5/6; Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and C showing laminar distribution.

claim: The proportion of EYFP+ cells in L2/3, L4 and L5/6 was comparable between EGIns and pRIns.

claim: Approximately 60% of EGIns were positive for SST.
source: In agreement with the temporal bias in the origins of the interneuron subgroups (Hu et al., 2017; Miyoshi et al., 2010; Miyoshi et al., 2007; Rudy et al., 2011),~60% of EGIns were positive for SST, and the proportion was much higher than that of pRIns (EGIns, 60.1 ± 3.7%, n = 7 mice; pRIns, 35.2 ± 1.7%, n = 6 mice; p<0.001, two-tailed unpaired t-test; Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The proportion of SST-positive cells was much higher in EGIns than in pRIns (60.1 ± 3.7% vs 35.2 ± 1.7%, p<0.001).

claim: The peak amplitudes of mIPSCs were indistinguishable between EGIns and pRIns at P5-7 (17.6 ± 1.0 pA vs 15.3 ± 0.7 pA, p=0.070).
source: We found that the frequency of mEPSCs and mIPSCs of EGIns was significantly higher than that of pRIns (EGIns, 1.9 ± 0.3 Hz for mEPSCs, n = 35 cells, 0.7 ± 0.1 Hz for mIPSCs, n = 30 cells; pRIns, 0.7 ± 0.1 Hz for mEPSCs, n = 37 cells, 0.5 ± 0.1 Hz for mIPSCs, n = 39 cells; p<0.001 for mEPSCs, p=0.040 for mIPSCs, Mann-Whitney U test; Figure 3E and G), while the peak amplitudes of mEPSCs and mIPSCs were indistinguishable between EGIns and pRIns (EGIns, 18.1 ± 1.2 pA for mEPSCs, n = 35 cells, 17.6 ± 1.0 pA for mIPSCs, n = 30 cells; pRIns, 16.5 ± 0.9 pA for mEPSCs, n = 37 cells, 15.3 ± 0.7 pA for mIPSCs, n = 39 cells; p=0.392 for mEPSCs, p=0.070 for mIPSCs, Mann-Whitney U test; Figure 3F and H ).

claim: The frequency of mEPSCs was comparable between dEGIns and sEGIns.

claim: The frequency of mIPSCs was comparable between dEGIns and sEGIns.

claim: Approximately 34.0% (18 out of 53) of EGIns formed unidirectional or bidirectional synaptic connections with excitatory neurons at P5-7.
source: We found ~34.0% (18 out of 53) of EGIns formed unidirectional or bidirectional synaptic connections with excitatory neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by dual whole-cell patch-clamp recording data.

claim: The proportion of synaptic connections in EGIn-PC pairs was significantly higher than in pRIn-PC pairs (34.0% vs 14.3%, p=0.010).
source: The proportion of synaptic connections in EGIn-PC pairs was significantly higher than in pRIn-PC pairs (pRIn-PC pairs, 14.3%, 11 out of 77; two-tailed Fisher's exact test, p=0.010; Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by dual whole-cell patch-clamp recording data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: EGIns have greater synaptic connectivity than pRIns at the early postnatal stages.
source: Together, these results suggest that EGIns have greater synaptic connectivity than pRIns at the early postnatal stages.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the synaptic connection probability data.

claim: Spontaneous synchronous network activity has been found throughout the developing neocortex and plays a critical role in neocortical development.
source: Spontaneous synchronous network activity has been found throughout the developing neocortex, and plays a critical role in neocortical development (Bando et al., 2016; Kasyanov et al., 2004; Kirkby et al., 2013; Mohajerani and Cherubini, 2006; Vargas et al., 2013; Voigt et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Giant depolarizing potentials (GDPs) represent a primordial form of synchrony between neurons in the immature neocortex.
source: In the immature neocortex, giant depolarizing potentials (GDPs) represent a primordial form of synchrony between neurons (Allène et al., 2008; Rheims et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Approximately 15.3% of EGIns could significantly affect GDP frequency at P5-7.
source: We found ~15.3% of EGIns could significantly affect GDP frequency (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by dual whole-cell patch-clamp recording data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: A lone pRIn exhibited significant effect on GDP frequency (1 out of 53, p=0.019 compared to EGIns).
source: In contrast, a lone pRIn exhibited significant effect on GDP frequency (EGIn, 9 out of 59; pRIn, 1 out of 53; two-tailed Fisher's exact test, p=0.019; Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by dual whole-cell patch-clamp recording data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The proportion of EGIns that significantly affect GDP frequency was comparable between P5–7 and P8–10 (p=1.000).
source: Therefore, we further compared the impacts of EGIns on GDPs between two sequential postnatal periods: P5-P7 and P8-P10, and found that the proportion of EGIns that significantly affect GDP frequency was comparable between P5–5 and P8–10 (P5–7, 9 out of 59; P8–10, 10 out of 67; two-tailed Fisher's exact test, p=1.000; Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by dual whole-cell patch-clamp recording data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: EGIns at P5–7 preferentially increased GDP frequency when stimulated, whereas EGIns at P8–10 preferentially decreased GDP frequency when stimulated (p=0.023).
source: Interestingly, we observed that EGIns at P5–7 preferentially increased GDP frequency when stimulated, whereas EGIns at P8–10 preferentially decreased GDP frequency when stimulated (P5–7, 7 cells showed increase versus 2 cells showed decrease; P8–10, 2 cells showed increase versus 8 cells showed decrease; two-tailed Fisher's exact test, p=0.023; Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by dual whole-cell patch-clamp recording data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The impact of EGIns on GDPs undergoes a switch from excitatory to inhibitory, which might correlate with the excitation-to-inhibition switch of GABAergic action.
source: These observations indicate that the impact of EGIns on GDPs undergoes a switch from excitatory to inhibitory, which might correlate with the excitation-to-inhibition switch of GABAergic action.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that EGIns increase GDP frequency at P5-7 but decrease it at P8-10, and is speculative regarding the mechanism.

claim: GABAergic neurotransmission undergoes a functional switch from excitatory to inhibitory during the developmental time window during which GDPs occur.
source: In the developmental time window during which GDPs occur, GABAergic neurotransmission undergoes a functional switch from excitatory to inhibitory (Ben-Ari, 2014; Ben-Ari et al., 2007; Dehorter et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: DT treatment effectively ablates EGIns and pRIns in the neocortex at early postnatal stages, reducing their densities to approximately 5% of that seen in saline-treated mice at P5.
source: 24 hr after the last DT administration (P5), we found the densities of both EGIns and pRIns in DT-treated mice were reduced to ~5% of that seen in saline-treated mice in the somatosensory neocortex (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: The density of caspase-3-positive cells in the somatosensory neocortex was similar between DT-injected CD1 mice and saline-injected CD1 mice at P5.
source: To further explore whether DT administration leads to non-Cre-expressing cell death, we labeled dying cells with caspase-3 and compared their densities between DT-injected CD1 mice and saline-injected CD1 mice at P5. We found the density of caspase-3-positive cells in the somatosensory neocortex was similar between DT-injected CD1 mice and saline-injected CD1 mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), indicating that the effect of DT is specific for Cre-expressing cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The effect of DT is specific for Cre-expressing cells.
source: To further explore whether DT administration leads to non-Cre-expressing cell death, we labeled dying cells with caspase-3 and compared their densities between DT-injected CD1 mice and saline-injected CD1 mice at P5. We found the density of caspase-3-positive cells in the somatosensory neocortex was similar between DT-injected CD1 mice and saline-injected CD1 mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), indicating that the effect of DT is specific for Cre-expressing cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that DT does not increase caspase-3 positive cells in non-Cre mice.

claim: The proportion of ablated neurons among total interneurons was estimated to be less than 0.4%.
source: In addition, compared with the density of GABAergic interneurons in the somatosensory neocortex of GAD67-GFP (Δneo) transgenic mice, we estimated the proportion of ablated neurons among total interneurons to be less than 0.4%.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with GAD67-GFP mice data.

claim: The average GDP frequency in EGIn-DT mice was significantly lower than in pRIn-DT and WT-DT mice at P5-7 (0.071 ± 0.009 Hz vs 0.092 ± 0.008 Hz vs 0.102 ± 0.008 Hz).
source: We observed that the average GDP frequency in EGIn-DT mice was significantly lower than in pRIn-DT and WT-DT mice (EGIn-DT, 0.071 ± 0.009 Hz, n = 63 cells from seven mice; pRIn-DT, 0.092 ± 0.008 Hz, n = 43 cells from four mice; WT-DT, 0.102 ± 0.008 Hz, n = 58 cells from seven mice; EGIn-DT versus pRIn-DT, p=0.016, EGIn-DT versus WT-DT, p=0.034, Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's Multiple Comparison test; Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The average GDP frequency exhibited no significant difference between pRIn-DT and WT-DT mice (p=0.493).

evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: EGIns contribute to spontaneous neocortical network synchronization at early postnatal stages.
source: These results indicate that EGIns contribute to spontaneous neocortical network synchronization at early postnatal stages.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the GDP frequency data after EGIn ablation.

claim: Pyramidal neurons in layer 5 of the somatosensory cortex of EGIn-DT mice exhibited normal morphological and intrinsic electrophysiological properties at P5–7 in contrast with pRIn-DT and WT-DT mice.

claim: The frequency of mIPSCs in EGIn-DT mice was significantly lower than in pRIn-DT and WT-DT mice at P5-7.

evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: The frequency of mEPSCs was indistinguishable between EGIn-DT, pRIn-DT and WT-DT mice at P5-7.

evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6G.

evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: EGIns are critical for proper spontaneous network synchronization and inhibitory synaptic transmission in the early postnatal neocortex.
source: These data suggest that EGIns are critical for proper spontaneous network synchronization and inhibitory synaptic transmission in the early postnatal neocortex.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the GDP frequency and mIPSC frequency data after EGIn ablation.

claim: The connection probability from non-EGIns to PCs was significantly higher in EGIn-EYFP mice (control) than in EGIn-ablated mice (DTR) at P5-7 (p=0.008).

claim: EGIns ablation reduces inhibitory synaptic formation from non-EGIns to PCs at the early postnatal stage.
source: Our data showed that the connection probability from non-EGIns to PCs was significantly higher in EGIn-EYFP mice (control) than in EGIn-ablated mice (DTR) (two-tailed Fisher's exact test, p=0.008; Figure 7D), indicating that EGIns ablation reduces inhibitory synaptic formation from non-EGIns to PCs at the early postnatal stage.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the connection probability data.

claim: The strength of non-EGIns→PCs uIPSCs did not exhibit significant change between control and DTR mice (26.2 ± 9.6 pA vs 45.5 ± 11.7 pA, p=0.223).

claim: EGIns regulate synaptic formation and presynaptic transmitter release from non-EGIns to PCs at the early postnatal stage.
source: Together, these results suggest EGIns regulate synaptic formation and presynaptic transmitter release from non-EGIns to PCs at the early postnatal stage.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the connection probability and PPR data after EGIn ablation.

claim: Pioneer interneurons in the neocortex, by contributing to neuronal synchrony at early postnatal stages, could play an important role in the wiring of immature cortical circuits.
source: Our findings suggest that pioneer interneurons in the neocortex, by contributing to neuronal synchrony at early postnatal stages, could play an important role in the wiring of immature cortical circuits.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results presented in the study.

claim: Unlike perisomatic-targeting PV interneurons, SST-expressing interneurons preferentially target distal dendrites of pyramidal neurons, and precisely control the efficacy and plasticity of glutamatergic inputs.
source: Unlike perisomatic-targeting PV interneurons, SST-expressing interneurons preferentially target distal dendrites of pyramidal neurons, and precisely control the efficacy and plasticity of glutamatergic inputs (Higley, 2014; Yavorska and Wehr, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SST-expressing interneurons play important roles in cortical circuit development.
source: Accumulating evidence suggests that SST-expressing interneurons play important roles in cortical circuit development (Fee et al., 2017; Liguz-Lecznar et al., 2016; Tuncdemir et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: EGIns transiently acquired their remarkable morphophysiological attributes at early postnatal stages, and exhibited comparable properties to pRIns with respect to their morphology and electrophysiology at adolescence (P15–20).
source: First, EGIns transiently acquired their remarkable morphophysiological attributes at early postnatal stages, and exhibited comparable properties to pRIns with respect to their morphology and electrophysiology at adolescence (P15–20).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing EGIns and pRIns at different developmental stages.

claim: EGIns received a significant increase in both excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs compared with pRIns at early postnatal stages.
source: Second, EGIns received a significant increase in both excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs compared with pRIns at early postnatal stages.
evidence: This claim is supported by mEPSC and mIPSC frequency data.

claim: The distinct properties of EGIns might contribute to their higher propensity to support the emergence of network oscillations and regulate cortical circuit development.
source: Taken together, these distinct properties of EGIns might contribute to their higher propensity to support the emergence of network oscillations and regulate cortical circuit development.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the functional implications of EGIn properties.

claim: Two distinct network oscillations, cortical early network oscillations (cENOs) and cortical giant depolarizing potentials (cGDPs), were observed in the developing neocortex.
source: Two distinct network oscillations, cortical early network oscillations (cENOs) and cortical giant depolarizing potentials (cGDPs), were observed in the developing neocortex (Allène et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The network oscillations recorded in neocortical layer five during P5–10 are mainly cGDPs based on frequency (~0.1 Hz) and synchronicity duration (200–300 ms).
source: We noted two features of the network oscillations which were reflected in recording layer five neurons during P5–10: (i) the frequency is ∼0.1 Hz, (ii) the synchronicity duration is 200–300 ms, which suggest that the network oscillations we recorded in neocortical layer five during P5–10 are mainly cGDPs (Allène et al., 2008; Ito, 2016; Rheims et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the characteristics of the recorded oscillations and supported by citations.

claim: Approximately 1/6 of EGIns in neocortical layer five could independently alter the frequency of spontaneous network synchronization when stimulated.
source: We observed ∼1/6 of EGIns in neocortical layer five could independently alter the frequency of spontaneous network synchronization when stimulated.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from GDP recordings.

claim: The proportion of EGIns that can alter network synchronization is much lower than reported in the hippocampus and entorhinal cortex.
source: The proportion is much lower than reported in the hippocampus and entorhinal cortex (Mòdol et al., 2017; Picardo et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim compares the current findings with previous literature.

claim: A single EGIn in neocortical layer five did not obviously trigger GDPs when stimulated, unlike hippocampal hub interneurons.
source: Moreover, unlike hippocampal hub interneurons (Picardo et al., 2011), we did not observe a single EGIn in neocortical layer five that could obviously trigger GDPs when stimulated.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations and comparison with previous literature.

claim: The differences between neocortical and hippocampal EGIns might be due to distinct brain structures, or methodological differences between patch-clamp recording and multineuron calcium imaging.
source: These differences might be due to distinct brain structures, or methodological differences between this (patch-clamp recording) and previous studies (multineuron calcium imaging) (Li et al., 1994; Mòdol et al., 2017; Namiki et al., 2013; Picardo et al., 2011; Radnikow et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential reasons for observed differences.

claim: EGIns are a heterogeneous population.
source: Furthermore, it is important to consider that EGIns are a heterogeneous population.
evidence: This is a statement based on the observed diversity in EGIn properties.

claim: It is unclear whether the subpopulation of EGIns that can single-handedly alter network dynamics represents one or more morpho-physiological subtypes of interneurons.
source: It is also unclear whether the subpopulation of EGIns that can single-handedly alter network dynamics represents one or more morpho-physiological subtypes of interneurons.
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging a limitation of the current study.

claim: Determining the subtypes of the subpopulation of EGIns that alter network dynamics is experimentally challenging since most interneurons during the period of GDP generation have not yet developed the characteristics that identify and classify them in adulthood.
source: However, determining the subtypes of this subpopulation of EGIns is experimentally challenging since most interneurons during the period of GDP generation have not yet developed the characteristics that identify and classify them in adulthood.
evidence: This is a statement explaining a technical limitation based on developmental biology knowledge.

claim: Early-generated interneurons shape synaptic wiring during the first postnatal week.
source: A major finding in this study is that early-generated interneurons shape synaptic wiring during the first postnatal week.
evidence: This is a summary statement of a major finding supported by the ablation experiments.

claim: Ablation of EGIns after P2 impaired the development of GABAergic synaptic inputs to layer five pyramidal neurons at P5–7, but did not alter their morphological and intrinsic electrophysiological properties.
source: We found that ablation of EGIns after P2 impaired the development of GABAergic synaptic inputs to layer five pyramidal neurons at P5–7, but did not alter their morphological and intrinsic electrophysiological properties.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ablation experiments.

claim: The reduction of inhibitory synaptic inputs onto pyramidal neurons after EGIn ablation is unlikely due to the decrease in the number of GABAergic neurons because EGIns are a very sparse cell population in the neocortex.
source: Although GABAergic neurons were deleted, the reduction of inhibitory synaptic inputs onto pyramidal neurons is unlikely due to the decrease in the number of GABAergic neurons for two reasons. First, EGIns are a very sparse cell population in the neocortex (Figure 1B) (Picardo et al., 2011; Villette et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the sparse distribution of EGIns and supported by citations.

claim: In the absence of a similar number of pRIns, layer five pyramidal neurons received normal inhibitory and excitatory synaptic inputs.
source: Second, in the absence of a similar number of pRIns, layer five pyramidal neurons received normal inhibitory and excitatory synaptic inputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from pRIn ablation experiments.

claim: One potential mechanism by which EGIns regulate inhibitory synapse formation could involve EGIns facilitating synchronized activity, which in turn promotes inhibitory synapse formation.
source: We speculate that one potential mechanism could involve EGIns in early postnatal stages that facilitate synchronized activity, which in turn promotes inhibitory synapse formation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a potential mechanism.

claim: The absence of EGIns, but not pRIns, could significantly reduce the frequency of GDPs in the first postnatal week.
source: Indeed, we found that the absence of EGIns, but not pRIns, could significantly reduce the frequency of GDPs in the first postnatal week.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ablation experiments.

claim: Alteration of GDP dynamics at early postnatal stages can modulate synaptic efficacy.
source: Moreover, in agreement with our speculation, previous studies suggest that alteration of GDP dynamics at early postnatal stages can modulate synaptic efficacy (Al-Muhtasib et al., 2018; Griguoli and Cherubini, 2017; Kasyanov et al., 2004; Mohajerani et al., 2007; Vargas et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Using current genetic strategy, EGIns were ablated not only in the neocortex but also in other brain regions (e.g., thalamus, striatum, hippocampus, etc.).
source: Nevertheless, it is important to note that using current genetic strategy, EGIns were ablated not only in the neocortex but also in other brain regions (e.g., thalamus, striatum, hippocampus, etc.).
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging a limitation of the experimental approach.

claim: Certain defects of synaptic development in the neocortex may relate to the alteration of afferent inputs from other brain regions where EGIns were also ablated.
source: Thus, we cannot exclude the possibility that certain defects of synaptic development in the neocortex may relate to the alteration of afferent inputs from these brain regions.
evidence: This is a speculative statement acknowledging a potential confound in the interpretation.

claim: Results from this study may be particularly important for understanding cell-type-specific network dysfunctions in neurodevelopmental disorders.
source: Given that disruptions of GABAergic circuitry at several points can contribute to neurodevelopmental disorders, results from this study may be particularly important for our understanding of cell-type-specific network dysfunctions in these disorders.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential implications of the findings.
